newsitem.title: USA: Swiss envoy says Nazi victims' claims too high.
newsitem.headline: Swiss envoy says Nazi victims' claims too high.

text.p: Switzerland's ambassador to Washington said on Wednesday the figure of $20 billion that Holocaust survivors were trying to recover from Swiss banks looked wildly exaggerated and the real sum involved was likely to prove far lower.

Envoy Carlo Jagmetti disputed the figures cited in class action suits filed this month in New York at a news conference in which he appealed for an end to "misrepresentations and distortions" of Swiss handling of assets seized by the Nazis.

A $20 billion suit was filed on Oct. 3 by Romanian Holocaust survivor Gizella Weisshaus against a group of Swiss banks for allegedly refusing to return victims' money, jewelry and other assets. A second suit for an unspecified sum was brought on behalf of five plaintiffs on Oct. 21.

"What is of course amazing is the figure," Jagmetti said. "But we were used to extraordinary figures in other cases and we'll see what happens. For me I must say these figures are just really speculative."
"There is one real problem in all this, (which) is that once we have the truth established, it might not be sensational ... and the figures might be much lower than many people thought," he added.

Switzerland has set up three panels to study Swiss banks' handling of accounts left by Jewish victims of the Holocaust and wealth stashed by Nazi Germany. An ombudsman is also processing individual claims, although a U.S. Jewish group charged on Monday he had not so far returned a single cent.

The mounting furor, which has thrown a harsh light on neutral Switzerland's actions during and after World War Two, stems in part from hearings by the U.S. Senate Banking Committee headed by New York Republican Alfonse D'Amato.

Jagmetti said Switzerland rejected D'Amato's charge that it had deceived the world for 50 years over the affair, but he described the hearings as "fair game -- it's a political game that has to be played".

He conceded that "psychological errors" were made by Swiss banks who dealt with past claimants and said it was "just unacceptable" for them to ask for death certificates of people killed in Nazi death camps, as heirs of victims have alleged.

"On the other hand, if you are a customer of a bank, you would like your bank to handle its business seriously and you don't expect your bank to pay money to anybody just coming and claiming without any proof," he said.

Jagmetti said he understood why Weisshaus and others had alleged that Swiss banks were trying to delay the issue until all the claimants had died. "I think the only thing we can do is to reassure them that we are at work." he said.
In a prepared statement clearly aimed at trying to improve Switzerland's image in the United States, the envoy hit out at accusations he said had been made before the facts were in.

Jagmetti rejected claims that a panel of Swiss historians trying to get to the bottom of the matter would take five years to report. Five years was the period for which the Swiss parliament was lifting bank secrecy laws, he said.

He also said a 1949 agreement with Poland, in which assets held by Swiss banks which belonged to Polish Nazi victims were handed over to the Polish government, was not secret as has been reported, and was covered by the press at the time.

Jagmetti also disputed an Oct. 24 New York Times report that assets of Holocaust victims were used to compensate Swiss citizens whose property in the then communist bloc had been nationalized. Swiss researcher Peter Hug, quoted in the report, had denied this, he said.
He said it was "imperative that misrepresentations and distortions of an issue which is in itself sufficiently sensitive should not stand in the way of the truth".
